input.body:
## Summary

Shield Turrets treated active-array membership as parentage, reacquired during trigger, and applied Setup values to rejected births. This broke the recovered cached-reference contracts. The layer now retains physical target/home references and the source's cached-avatar read interruption.

```text
parent poll → EnemyAim → timer → trigger using existing rotation
cached target = avatar → missing inner_mc read → end this listener
closed birth gate → same unparented constructor object, no Setup
```

Layer 4 of the five-layer stack, based on [#137](https://github.com/ianwijma/open-bubble-tank/pull/137). Hold master for the last combined PR and its current-head gate.

## Evidence

- **Before:** five initial contract regressions fail; an additional missing-home regression rejects UID fallback.
  **After:** all seven new contract cases pass, including actual-parent shielding, detached target transforms, signed-zero/random aim, trigger ordering, home parentage and rejected defaults.
- Three controlled probes call original methods on original objects in Ruffle. They preserve both original ABC payloads and all other nonbinding tag payloads, verified independently. Normal and named-part avatars produce ReferenceError #1069 in the original EnemyAim; the rejected-birth probe returns the same unparented zero-pose object with NaN speed and constructor defaults. Loaded JS/WASM bytes match installed runtime bytes. These are controlled calls, not an ordinary original cached encounter or Adobe proof.
- Formatting, TypeScript and all 929 unit tests / 8,513 assertions pass.
- Production build and all 18 affected mock/supplied-art browser cases pass with zero skips, flaky results or page errors. The turret gallery retains its six previous clip/frame/paint checks and adds cached shield/counter/sound/artwork checks. Both modes were inspected; all owned probe and validation processes stopped.
- [The source/runtime reference](https://github.com/ianwijma/open-bubble-tank/blob/stack/wave-selection-04-turret-contracts/docs/shield-turret-retention-reference.md) records commands, hashes, build, observed results, source-derived inferences and remaining limits. No SWF/probe output, original media or build artifacts are committed.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

No saved-data migration.

**Blast Radius:** gameplay

Cached avatar targeting now interrupts the modeled listener as the recovered call chain requires; shielding from an old parented turret remains. Physical removal, separate artwork and source-scoped RemoveBullet stay distinct. The optional saved-enemy caller is proven; builtin catalogs contain no 4032. Arbitrary matrices, complete constructor/event/RNG scheduling, ordinary earned encounters and synchronized original/Adobe/full-game parity remain unfinished.

The existing `stack/**` deployment control remains in place.

Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration.

Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required.

## Invariants

- Simulation units are pixels/frame, degrees, and frame counters. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta.
- The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions.
- Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP.
- The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`.
- Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate.
- Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating.
- Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances.
- Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file.
- Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations.
- Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions.

## Extending the game

- Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view. Keep part IDs stable for code compatibility.
- Keep data importers reproducible. Derived JSON is checked in so the research repository is not a production dependency.
- `services/extensions.ts` contains typed interfaces for community tanks, accounts, parts packs, medals, platform stats, and ads. Replace the offline adapters to restore those systems without adding endpoint logic to gameplay.
- `services/profile.ts` validates versioned local JSON. The persistence boundary is replaceable; no component needs to know Flash SharedObject internals.
- `services/tank-code.ts` implements the original AES-128-ECB/PKCS7 tank format using Web Crypto's CBC primitive blockwise. It is a compatibility codec, not an account/security mechanism.
- A future renderer can consume the same `World`; a replay/test harness can call `World.step` with seeded input without a DOM.

# Babysit PR

Many repos have AI review bots. They're helpful, even if they are not always
right.

## Waiting

Never write your own watcher, polling loop, or `sleep` loop. Use one watcher
per PR: `watch_pull_request` in T3 Code, `pr-wait` everywhere else. Never run
both on the same PR. Every watcher on a GitHub account shares one rate limit.

### In T3 Code: `watch_pull_request`

Handle the existing checks and comments first. Then call
`watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you with a message when
a check fails, the required checks pass, someone comments or reviews, or the
branch conflicts.

- **Only the thread that owns the PR watches it.** If you are a delegated
  child task (a reviewer, a Sol round, any `delegate_task` child), never call
  `watch_pull_request`. The parent owns the PR. Do not watch PRs you are not
  working on.
- **A wake is news, not a merge decision.** Check the merge gate yourself.
- **Unwatch when you hand off.** A watched thread stays in Working and out of
  the user's inbox. When you stop (ready, blocked, or asking the user a question),
  call `unwatch_pull_request` first. A merge or close ends the watch on its
  own.
- **"Stopped watching, could not read it"** usually means GitHub's rate limit
  is used up. Run `gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql` before you
  watch again. If `remaining` is near 0, wait for `reset` with one background
  command, then watch again. Never watch again in a tight loop.

### Everywhere else: `pr-wait`

Wait with `scripts/pr-wait` from this skill's directory (use its absolute
path).

```bash
pr-wait <pr> [--repo owner/name] [--until ready|green|any-change]
```

It prints one line per real event. It exits 0 when the `--until` condition is
met or the PR merges, 1 when it needs you (a required check failed, conflicts,
unresolved threads, PR closed), and 2 on bad input.

- `ready` (default): required checks green, Greptile or Macroscope reviewed the
  head, and no unresolved threads. Use this to babysit.
- `green`: required checks only. Use it when the repo has no Greptile or
  Macroscope.
- `any-change`: exit on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it with the Monitor tool (`timeout_ms: 3600000`), so each
line wakes you. Without a monitor, run it as one long command. It ends on its
own.

Start it again after you push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume.
It remembers what it already reported, so nothing that arrived in between is
lost. If it says another pid already watches the PR, do not start a second one.
Kill the old one only if its events do not reach you.

With either watcher: when an event needs no action, end your turn without a
message. Never post or say "still waiting".

## GitHub rate limits

`gh pr create`, `gh pr view`, and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL. When GraphQL is
used up, the REST limit is separate and usually still has room. Use
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` to read a PR, and
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs` for checks.

## Reviews

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push. Verify every bot
finding against the source before changing code. Fix real findings and CI
failures, distinguish repository failures from infrastructure flakes, and reply
with a written reason when dismissing false positives.

If the repo has `.macroscope/check-run-agents/*.md`, read those rules before you
reply to a Macroscope finding. Its findings cite them.

CodeRabbit is advisory. Treat its findings like any other finding, but never
wait for it and never hold a merge for it.

If a review bot leaves feedback you believe is not worth addressing, reply with
a written reason and resolve the comment. Use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill
for every comment posted on the user's behalf.

Screenshots and videos help as well, when you have a way to upload them.

Keep the PR at the size the user's goal needs. Review loops tend to grow a
PR one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the intended case.
Decline the rest with a written reason, and list them as follow-ups:
unneeded tests, guards for edge cases that do not matter, extra integration
or compatibility, and small performance costs. Prefer the fix that deletes or
narrows code.

## Base branch and merging

Keep an eye on changes to `main` and rebase when needed. `pr-wait` reports when
new base commits touch this PR's files, and when the PR becomes BEHIND or DIRTY.
`watch_pull_request` reports conflicts only, so check for BEHIND yourself
before you call the PR ready.
If an overlapping PR makes this one obsolete, stop monitoring, report it to the
user, and ask before closing the PR unless closure was explicitly authorized.

If nothing has changed, stay quiet rather than posting filler comments. Stop
when `pr-wait` exits 0, or in T3 Code when the merge gate passes on the latest
head. Merge only when the user explicitly requested it;
otherwise report that the PR is ready. Right before a merge, run `git fetch` and
check the PR again. Never merge when it is BEHIND or DIRTY, or when base commits
that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files. Rebase, push, and
wait for green again.

# File PR

Before filing, check whether a PR for this branch already exists. Review the
diff locally against the base branch (usually `origin/main`) to make sure its
contents match the goal.

PR titles usually become commit messages, so follow the repository's title
conventions. Look at recently merged PRs and Git history for examples. Prefer a
concise, human-readable title that explains why the change matters:

BAD

> ❌ perf(server): negotiate permessage-deflate on the websocket

GOOD

> ✅ perf(server): cut websocket frame size by 70%+ with gzipping

Open the description with a simple explanation of the problem based on the
user's original prompt, then briefly explain the solution. Do not lead with an
implementation inventory:

BAD

> ❌ Removed implicit workspace carry-over from every "new thread" entry point (cmd+n / cmd+shift+o, sidebar v1/v2 buttons, command palette). New threads inherit only the project from context; branch, worktree, and env mode always come from the configured defaults. # Architecture

## Engine choice

[PixiJS](https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/application) supplies the WebGL renderer and scene graph. The game does not need a rigid-body physics engine, a tile map, or an entity framework: the recovered simulation uses authored tank parts, point-against-art collision, independent velocity axes, and frame timers. Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration.

Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required.

## Ownership and flow

1. `AssetGate` accepts a local file or initializes procedural mock artwork.
2. `AssetPack` extracts images, sounds, vectors, font outlines, and sprite placements. It composes frozen previews and shared vector-leaf textures. It never executes ABC/ActionScript or calls retired endpoints.
3. `GameShell` owns the local profile, screen navigation, dialogs, and a `World` instance.
4. `GameViewport` owns input listeners, the Pixi renderer and cleanup. `MainStage` drives the shared `StageRuntime` fixed-step clock. Input is cleared on blur and gameplay pauses when hidden.
5. `World.step` advances one original game frame. `weapons.ts`, `projectiles.ts`, `actor-movement.ts`, `waves.ts`, and `tank.ts` implement separate systems. Beam contact, healer patient ownership, turret construction, and status callbacks/clocks are isolated in `beams.ts`, `healing.ts`, `turrets.ts`, and `status.ts`. Rendering and browser storage are absent from these rules.
6. `GameRenderer` positions the camera at the avatar, draws fields/entities/projectiles/pickups/effects, and updates `SwfSymbolView` display lists. `AssetPack` supplies matching animated alpha-mask hit tests.
7. React observes a revision counter, approximately ten updates per second at 50 FPS; it does not render every simulation frame.

Per-frame rendering uses refs and stage subscriptions, while `GameShell` owns screen changes and the guarded overlay. A new menu instance resets its intro; closing a child pane preserves its title timeline.

## Invariants

- Simulation units are pixels/frame, degrees, and frame counters. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta.
- The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions.
- Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP.
- The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`.
- Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate.
- Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating.
- Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances.
- Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file.
- Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations.
- Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions.

## Extending the game

- Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view. Keep part IDs stable for code compatibility.
- Keep data importers reproducible. Derived JSON is checked in so the research repository is not a production dependency.
- `services/extensions.ts` contains typed interfaces for community tanks, accounts, parts packs, medals, platform stats, and ads. Replace the offline adapters to restore those systems without adding endpoint logic to gameplay.
- `services/profile.ts` validates versioned local JSON. The persistence boundary is replaceable; no component needs to know Flash SharedObject internals.
- `services/tank-code.ts` implements the original AES-128-ECB/PKCS7 tank format using Web Crypto's CBC primitive blockwise. It is a compatibility codec, not an account/security mechanism.
- A future renderer can consume the same `World`; a replay/test harness can call `World.step` with seeded input without a DOM.

## Asset lifetime

# Five-PR delivery stacks

The current user policy is to accumulate five dependent PRs before integrating the
batch into master. Keep each layer coherent and reviewable. Assemble five layers
before the final combined merge to master.

```text
master ← PR1 ← PR2 ← PR3 ← PR4 ← PR5
```

The bottom PR targets master. Each later PR targets the preceding layer's branch,
so its review shows that layer's change. Use `stack/<batch>-<layer>-<description>`
for batch branches, including the first layer when conserving previews. Preserve the
legacy recreation checkpoint unchanged.

While an earlier layer runs CI, build the next dependent layer when its scope is
clear. Up to five layers may be in flight together. Keep fixes on their owning
branch, propagate them through dependent layers, and validate each resulting head.
Do not open a sixth layer or fold a partial batch into master merely to avoid a wait.

For each finalized PR, create an isolated get-green agent to inspect current-head
Actions and reviews, repair concrete failures and escalate uncertain fundamental
changes to the parent. Pending, missing or failed Actions is not green, but an
intermediate wait does not block assembling the later layers. The merge gate is the
last PR's complete combined head, with a successful named `Rules, build and mock
browser` job and no actionable review findings. Never remove assertions or suites
merely to obtain green checks.

Once five layers exist, assemble all changes on the last PR's branch and target that
PR directly at master. A dependent top branch already contains its ancestors; verify
that ancestry and fold in any missing layer or repair. Validate the final combined
head once instead of waiting for a new CI pass after every intermediate fold. Require
its complete current-head Actions/review gate before the single master merge. Earlier
open layers can target master so their included commits are accounted for by that
combined merge. If master changes during the batch, integrate it and validate the
resulting tree before the final merge. Verify the fetched head and resulting tree;
do not infer completion from a queued operation.

## Vercel deployment budget

Stacking alone does not suppress preview builds. `vercel.json` sets
`git.deploymentEnabled["stack/**"]` to false, using Vercel's supported minimatch branch
rules. Pushes to those batch branches therefore skip automatic Vercel deployments.
Unspecified branches retain their normal behavior, including master. Keeping every
layer under `stack/**` leaves the one master merge as the automatic production
deployment for a batch. A deliberate preview on another branch remains optional.

See [Vercel's Git configuration](https://vercel.com/docs/project-configuration/git-configuration).
Do not add a broad true rule overlapping `stack/**`: Vercel deploys when any matching
rule enables it. A deliberate intermediate preview skip is expected; continue to
require Actions and reviews. Only the previously observed daily deployment-quota
failure is waived. Investigate other actual deployment failures, and do not retry
deployments or change billing as a response to quota exhaustion.

Validate repository configuration before pushing and inspect provider feedback to
confirm the intended skip. Configuration validity alone does not prove that Vercel
honored the branch rule. No provider account, production-branch or billing setting is
changed by this repository rule.
